passage: After school in Nairobi, Omar minded his uncle's phone-accessory stall until six, the way he'd promised. Between customers, his phone buzzed. A classmate had sent a video of Kwame tripping on the stairs, his lunch spilling everywhere, with a crying-laughing caption. It already had dozens of views. Omar's thumb hovered over the forward button. Everyone would laugh; he'd look like he was in on it. Then he remembered Kwame helping him with maths last term. He didn't forward it. Instead he typed to the sender, "Not cool, delete it," and messaged Kwame: "Saw the video. It's nothing. You ok?" Kwame replied with one word: "thanks." Omar pocketed the phone, sold a charger to a woman in a hurry, and noted it in his uncle's book.

qa.q: Until what time did Omar mind his uncle's stall?
qa.a: Until six.

qa.q: What made Omar hesitate before choosing not to forward the video?
qa.a: He felt the pull to join in so he'd look like part of the group, but remembering Kwame's kindness made him feel uneasy about hurting him.

qa.q: What could Omar do if the video keeps spreading?
qa.a: He could tell a trusted teacher or adult so it can be removed, and keep checking in with Kwame.

qa.q: How might Kwame have felt receiving Omar's message?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed and hurt by the video, so a private, kind message would feel like support when he needed it.

grounding: Shows a teen balancing family duty with refusing to join online bullying and acting ethically online.

passage: The school's cyber club met in the computer lab on Wednesdays. This week, Gurleen showed everyone an anonymous "confessions" page where students posted rumours about classmates. One post named a Class 9 girl and her weight. Some of the club members laughed. Jasleen didn't. "We can't just watch this," she said. "People believe what they read." Gurleen shrugged. "It's anonymous. What can we do?" Jasleen pulled up the platform's report tool and walked them through it, then drafted a short note for the class groups: "Don't comment, don't share, report it." She also went to the counsellor's room after the bell to tell her about the page. That evening she changed her own passwords and turned off location on her photos, just in case.

qa.q: On which day did the cyber club meet?
qa.a: On Wednesdays.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen refuse to laugh at the post?
qa.a: She felt it was cruel and worried that people would believe the rumour, which could really hurt the Class 9 girl.

qa.q: Which of Jasleen's steps was most important, and why?
qa.a: Telling the counsellor, because an adult can act on the page and support the girl, beyond what reporting alone can do.

qa.q: How might the Class 9 girl feel if she saw the post?
qa.a: She would likely feel humiliated and exposed, so knowing classmates reported it instead of sharing it could make a real difference.

grounding: Shows a teen in a school setting practising online ethics, rejecting digital bullying and protecting her own privacy.

passage:
Dear Chaitanya,

Mummy says you got your first phone. Congratulations! Since I'm the big sister who made every mistake first, here's my short list.

Never share your password, even with your best friend. Mine "borrowed" my account in Class 8 and posted something silly as me. It took weeks to fix.

Before you post anything, imagine Nani reading it. If you'd cringe, don't post.

If someone in a group gets mocked, don't add a laughing emoji. Staying out isn't enough sometimes; say "stop" or tell a teacher.

Put the phone away by ten. Board exams are next year, and I learnt the hard way that sleep matters more than one more video.

And help Mummy with the shopping on Sundays. She won't say, but she's tired.

Love,
Charu didi

qa.q: What happened when Charu's friend borrowed her account in Class 8?
qa.a: The friend posted something silly as her, and it took weeks to fix.

qa.q: What does Charu's reminder about helping Mummy suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She is worried about their tired mother and wants Chaitanya to share family duties, not just enjoy his new phone.

qa.q: How could Chaitanya follow the 'imagine Nani reading it' test in practice?
qa.a: Chaitanya could pause before each post and ask, "Would I be comfortable with family seeing this?", deleting the draft if not.

qa.q: What would change if Charu simply gave Chaitanya a list of rules without her stories?
qa.a: Chaitanya might ignore them, because hearing her own mistakes makes the advice feel real and less like a lecture. 🙂

grounding: An older sister writes to a younger sibling about online ethics, reputation, sleep and family duties.

passage: 'Tanvir, you asked what I learned this year. Okay, one night. Somebody posted a video mocking our football team, and one of the players was my cousin. I typed a reply full of abuse, really nasty stuff about the guy's family. My thumb was on send. Then I thought: this will be online forever, with my name, Asif, right on it, and colleges look at this stuff. And Abbu would see it. I deleted it. Instead I messaged my cousin privately: "Ignore him, you played well." Next day I reported the video. That's it. Not dramatic. But I learned there's a gap between feeling something and posting it, and I have to live in that gap.'

qa.q: Who was the player in the mocked video?
qa.a: Asif's cousin.

qa.q: What was Asif worried about with a thumb on send?
qa.a: Asif worried the comment would stay online with that name on it, could affect how colleges see Asif, and that Abbu would see it.

qa.q: Which of Asif's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Messaging the cousin privately and reporting the video, because it supported the cousin and dealt with the post without adding more abuse.

qa.q: How might Asif's cousin have felt getting Asif's private message?
qa.a: Comforted and backed up, without being dragged into a public fight.

grounding: Shows a teenager protecting their reputation and choosing ethical online behaviour over an abusive reply.

passage: I'm Bidisha, and I sit next to Deepika. Here's what I've seen this term. She leaves at 1:30 on Wednesdays because she takes her Nani to her check-ups, and she copies the missed notes from me that evening without fail. When our class group started a poll ranking girls by looks, almost everyone voted, and I did too. Deepika posted one line: 'Not voting on people. Leaving this group.' Then she left. Some people called her dramatic. The next day the class teacher found out and the poll was deleted; I don't know if Deepika told her. When I asked, she just shrugged. 'I have Nani's appointments and physics. No time for that stuff.' I think it bothered her more than she said. Her ears were red.

qa.q: What time does Deepika leave on Wednesdays?
What might Deepika's red ears suggest about her shrug?
qa.a: They suggest she felt upset and embarrassed by the poll and people's reactions, more than her casual shrug showed.

qa.q: What could Bidisha do after seeing Deepika's stand?
qa.a: Bidisha could take back that vote and tell Deepika about agreeing, or tell a teacher if such polls start again.

qa.q: How might the girls ranked in the poll have been affected?
qa.a: They could feel judged and hurt by classmates; Deepika's refusal showed at least one person wouldn't take part.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager keeping family and study duties while refusing to join online bullying, seen by a classmate.

passage: Monday: a private photo of Gargi, taken at a sleepover, appeared in Seema's class group with a mocking caption. Seema, fifteen, felt sick. Tuesday: people kept forwarding it. A friend told Seema, "Just laugh, everyone is." She didn't forward it. She reported it in the app, messaged Gargi, "I'm with you. Want to tell Ma'am together?" and they went to the class teacher that afternoon. The teacher had it removed and spoke to the class. Wednesday: Seema also finished her maths assignment on time, even with everything going on, and slept early. Gargi sat with her at lunch.

qa.q: Where did the private photo appear?
qa.a: In Seema's class group.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when she first saw the photo?
qa.a: She felt sick and upset, knowing it was cruel to Gargi.

qa.q: What did Seema do right in handling it?
qa.a: She refused to forward it, reported it, supported Gargi and went to the teacher the same afternoon.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel when Seema messages her?
qa.a: Less alone and grateful to have someone on her side.

grounding: Shows a teenager rejecting online bullying, practising cyber ethics and still keeping up with her duties.

passage: "Saurabh, I'll tell you about the exam paper. When I, your Chetan Chacha, was sixteen, someone got the maths question paper the night before, and a photo went round our group. My friend said, 'Everyone's seen it. You'll be the only fool.' I sat with my phone for an hour, thumb over the image. I didn't open it. The next morning I told the principal, even though I knew people would hate me. The exam was cancelled and redone. Some boys didn't speak to me for months. But my name stayed clean, and that mattered more to me than marks."

qa.q: What went round young Chetan's group?
qa.a: A photo of the maths question paper.

qa.q: What was young Chetan feeling with his thumb over the image?
qa.a: He felt tempted and afraid of being the only one without it, but uneasy about cheating.

qa.q: What turning point in the story protected Chetan's reputation?
qa.a: Choosing not to open the photo and telling the principal the next morning.

qa.q: How might the boys who stopped speaking to Chetan have felt?
qa.a: Angry and resentful at having the exam redone, even though they had cheated.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a teenager he protected his reputation and practised digital ethics about a leaked paper.

passage: It was the night before the chemistry exam, and Sumit, seventeen, was also looking after his grandmother, who had a fever, because his parents were at a wedding. At ten, his friend Bhupen messaged: "Got the answers from a guy who knows someone. Want?" Sumit looked at his notes, then at his grandmother dozing on the sofa. He typed, "No thanks. And don't forward it." He checked her water, warmed the soup his mother had left out, and studied at the dining table until midnight, getting up every half hour to check on her. He went to bed tired but with a clear head.

qa.q: Who was Sumit looking after?
qa.a: His grandmother, who had a fever.

qa.q: What might Sumit have felt when Bhupen's message came?
qa.a: He probably felt tempted and stressed, but also uneasy about cheating.

qa.q: What made Sumit's night a responsible one?
qa.a: He refused the answers, cared for his grandmother as his mother had arranged, and studied honestly.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Sumit's reply?
qa.a: He might be annoyed or embarrassed, or it might make him rethink the answers too.

grounding: Shows a teenager balancing family duty, honest study and online ethics under time pressure.

passage: On Tuesday evening in the Indore flat, Gautam, fifteen, had three things: Dadaji's blood-pressure tablets to pick up from the chemist by seven, a history assignment due tomorrow, and a group chat buzzing. Some classmates were making a fake account to post jokes about Deepak Sir, their strict maths teacher. "Gautam, you're good at edits. Make the profile pic." He was tempted; he'd been scolded by Deepak Sir that morning. But he pictured Sir seeing it. He typed, "Not doing this. It's not okay," and muted the chat. Then he went to the chemist, gave Dadaji the tablets, and sat down with history. Later he told his mother about the fake account, and she said she would inform the class teacher.

qa.q: By what time did Gautam have to pick up the tablets?
qa.a: By seven.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when he was asked to make the profile picture?
qa.a: He felt tempted and still a little resentful about being scolded, but uneasy about hurting Deepak Sir.

qa.q: Which of Gautam's choices were responsible?
qa.a: Refusing to join the fake account, telling his mother about it, and still doing his duties for Dadaji and history.

qa.q: How might Deepak Sir be affected if the fake account had gone ahead?
qa.a: He could have been embarrassed and hurt, with his reputation damaged in front of students.

grounding: A teenager juggles family and school duties and refuses to help make a fake account mocking a teacher.

passage:
"Didi, look at this photo of Rishi falling off the bench. So funny. I'm posting it."
"Did Rishi say you could?"
"It's just a photo, Nandini Didi."
"Vaibhav. Would you want your worst photo up for the whole school?"
He paused. "No."
"So ask him."
"He'll say no."
"Then that's your answer."
Vaibhav groaned. "Also, can I give Rishi my phone password? He wants to use my account for the game."
"No. Passwords are like toothbrushes. Not for sharing."
"Ew."
"Exactly."
Vaibhav deleted the photo and texted Rishi instead: "Bro, you fell like a movie villain." Rishi replied with three laughing faces.

qa.q: What was Rishi doing in the photo?
qa.a: Falling off the bench.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when he said "He'll say no"?
qa.a: He felt reluctant and a little annoyed, wanting to post the photo even though he knew Rishi wouldn't like it.

qa.q: What two online rules did Nandini help Vaibhav think through?
qa.a: Asking before posting someone's photo, and not sharing passwords.

qa.q: How might Rishi feel about the private joke instead of a public post?
qa.a: Rishi likely enjoyed the private joke and was spared public embarrassment.

grounding: An older sister helps her brother think through consent before posting a photo and not sharing passwords.

passage: I'm Bhavna. In Class 9, some girls in my class started a joke about Tarun's weight in our group chat. I added one comment. Just one. A cartoon of a balloon. Everyone laughed. The next day, Tarun didn't come to school. Then he didn't come for three days. I couldn't eat properly. I kept looking at that balloon. On the fourth day, I told our class teacher what had happened in the chat, including my part. She spoke to the group and to Tarun's parents. I also said sorry to Tarun, face to face. He didn't say much. It's been a year. We're not close, but he nods at me now. I don't post anything about anyone without thinking twice anymore.

qa.q: What did Bhavna add to the chat?
qa.a: A cartoon of a balloon.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel when Tarun stopped coming to school?
qa.a: Bhavna felt guilty and anxious, unable to eat properly.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do to make things right?
qa.a: Told the class teacher, including Bhavna's own part, and apologised to Tarun face to face.

qa.q: How might Tarun have been affected by the chat?
qa.a: He was likely deeply hurt and humiliated, which may be why he missed school.

grounding: A teenager reflects on joining online bullying, reporting it and taking responsibility.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 9
Joseph came to me on Wednesday with a screenshot. A group chat had been sharing an edited photo of Rukmini with a mean caption. Joseph had been added to the chat and felt sick seeing it.
He told me he had not forwarded it. He had written in the group, "This is not okay, delete it," and then left. Two boys had called him a traitor.
I thanked him, told him he did the right thing, and reassured him he was not in trouble. I met Rukmini that afternoon with her class teacher, and we informed her parents and the parents of those who shared the image by evening. The photo was removed from the group.
I will check on both Rukmini and Joseph next week.

qa.q: What was being shared in the group chat?
qa.a: An edited photo of Rukmini with a mean caption.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when he saw the photo?
qa.a: He felt sick and upset, and then under pressure when two boys called him a traitor.

qa.q: What made the counsellor's response right?
qa.a: The counsellor thanked Joseph, acted the same afternoon, met Rukmini, informed parents and got the photo removed.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel when she learns what happened?
qa.a: Rukmini may feel hurt and embarrassed, but also supported that someone refused to share it and adults acted.

grounding: A counsellor records a teen rejecting online bullying and reporting it.

passage:
Friday
Weird day. Vikas asked if he could copy my physics assignment "just this once." I've let him before. This time I said no. My face went hot saying it.
He called me selfish and didn't sit with me at lunch.
Then in the evening I found out he'd put a fake review on the local bakery's page because they wouldn't give him a free pastry. He thought it was funny. I thought it was mean, and it's somebody's shop. I told him so on the phone. He hung up.
I told Mummy about the review. She said she'd mention it to his mother, calmly.
Some days being responsible just feels lonely. But I'd feel worse if I'd helped him cheat or laughed at the review.
Chetan

qa.q: What did Vikas do to the bakery?
qa.a: He put a fake review on the local bakery's page.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel saying no to Vikas?
qa.a: Chetan felt uncomfortable and a bit lonely; the face went hot.

qa.q: What would you advise Chetan now?
qa.a: Stay firm but friendly with Vikas, and let adults handle the review while Chetan keeps to honest work.

qa.q: How might the bakery owner feel about the fake review?
qa.a: The owner would likely feel hurt and worried, since a false review can damage a small shop.

grounding: A teen's diary on refusing to cheat and speaking up about online dishonesty.

passage: In their village in Mandya, Uma fed the cows before school and did her maths homework on the bus. At lunch her phone buzzed: someone had posted an edited photo of Parul in the class group, her face stuck on a buffalo, with laughing faces piling up underneath. A classmate nudged Uma. "Forward it to the other section." Uma didn't laugh. She typed in the group, "This isn't funny. Delete it," and left. Then she found Parul by the well, eyes red, and walked with her to Headmistress Kamalamma's office. The headmistress looked at the photo, called both classes together that afternoon, and had it deleted in front of her. She rang Parul's mother before the last bell.

qa.q: What had someone stuck Parul's face on in the edited photo?
qa.a: On a buffalo.

qa.q: Why didn't Uma laugh when the classmate nudged her?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and sympathetic, knowing the photo would hurt and humiliate Parul.

qa.q: What did Uma do that helped most, and why?
qa.a: Refusing to forward it, speaking up in the group and going with Parul to the headmistress got an adult to stop it the same day.

qa.q: What is it like for Parul when Uma finds her by the well?
qa.a: Parul, already hurt and embarrassed, likely feels less alone with someone walking beside her.

grounding: Shows a teenager balancing chores and study while refusing to share a bullying photo online and taking it to the headmistress.
